Explainable Cardiovascular Disease Prediction: Multi-Cohort Tabular Machine Learning, Generalization Audits, and Decision Curve Analysis

Under the Guidance of Rinky Chhatwani
Vansh Rawat, Drisha Chauhan, Karan Bheda, and Harsh Rathva
Department of Artificial Intelligence
Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology, Surat, Gujarat, India

Abstract—Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) represent the foremost cause of global mortality, accounting for approximately 17.9 million annual deaths according to the World Health Organization. While machine learning classifiers have promised enhanced risk detection, published healthcare AI literature frequently suffers from fatal methodological flaws: naive multi-center cohort pooling, severe data leakage during feature preprocessing, over-reliance on threshold-dependent accuracy, and an absence of clinical utility evaluation. In this paper, we formulate and validate a leakage-safe, multi-cohort tabular machine learning framework for CVD screening. Our research is grounded in two independently handled clinical datasets: a large primary-care screening cohort (Cardio70k, $N = 68,581$; 44,665 females and 23,916 males) and an international multi-center clinical cohort (Unified Clinical, $N = 1,918$ across five hospital centers: Mendeley Data India $N=1,000$, UCI Cleveland $N=303$, UCI Hungary $N=293$, UCI Long Beach VA $N=199$, and UCI Switzerland $N=123$). We benchmark generalized linear models, ensemble decision trees (Random Forest, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost), and deep tabular neural networks (Multi-Layer Perceptron, MLP) under repeated 5-fold stratified cross-validation and nested outer-fold selection. On Cardio70k, XGBoost attained champion discrimination (ROC-AUC: $0.8019 \pm 0.0027$, PR-AUC: $0.7828$, Brier score: $0.1802$), statistically outperforming the deep tabular neural network ($\Delta\text{ROC-AUC} = +0.0027$, 95% CI: $[0.0020, 0.0036]$, paired bootstrap $p < 0.001$). Under Leave-One-Source-Out (LOSO) multi-center stress testing, we uncover steep cross-border generalization decay, where models trained on Western hospital centers collapsed to near-random discrimination ($0.4937$ ROC-AUC) on the Indian cohort, demonstrating pronounced clinical covariate shift. Moving beyond discrimination, Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) proves a substantial positive Net Clinical Benefit ($+0.3246$ at threshold probability $p_t = 0.30$ vs. $+0.2782$ for universal treatment). Finally, model-agnostic permutation feature reliance and demographic subgroup auditing with exact 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals provide transparent validation of clinical alignment and algorithmic equity.

Index Terms—Cardiovascular disease, tabular machine learning, decision curve analysis, multi-center generalization, probability calibration, explainable AI, algorithmic fairness.

I. Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading contributor to global morbidity and mortality [1]. Standard primary-care screening tools, such as the Framingham Risk Score [2] and the European SCORE2 guidelines [3], employ multivariable parametric regressions fitted on historical epidemiological cohorts. Although clinically entrenched, these linear scoring systems cannot autonomously capture complex non-linear interactions among physiological biomarkers, such as the non-linear coupling between advancing age, arterial stiffening, and dyslipidemia.

In response, machine learning (ML) models have been widely investigated for automated CVD screening. However, contemporary translational AI reviews highlight persistent methodological vulnerabilities across published studies violating TRIPOD reporting guidelines [13]:

1) Naive Cohort Pooling: Disparate datasets collected across distinct hospital settings and healthcare systems are routinely concatenated into a single database. This masks severe institutional covariate shifts and produces overly optimistic validation figures that collapse when tested in real-world clinical practice.

2) Pervasive Data Leakage: Transformations such as standard scaling, outlier clipping, and missing value imputation are frequently executed over the entire dataset prior to cross-validation splits, transmitting target and distribution information from validation folds into model training.

3) Deep Learning Over-Complication: Highly parameterized neural networks are often deployed on tabular medical records without demonstrating statistical superiority over well-regularized tree-based models [11], [12].

4) Neglect of Clinical Utility: Evaluators predominantly report ROC-AUC, sensitivity, or accuracy at an arbitrary $0.5$ classification threshold, failing to quantify whether automated triaging provides positive Net Clinical Benefit over standard clinical intervention policies [6], [7].

To resolve these critical vulnerabilities, this study introduces an end-to-end, leak-free, and explainable cardiovascular prediction framework developed under the faculty guidance of Rinky Chhatwani at the Department of Artificial Intelligence, Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology, Surat. Our principal contributions are:

• Strict Cohort Segregation: Independent evaluation of a large screening cohort (Cardio70k, $N = 68,581$) and a multi-center diagnostic cohort (Unified Clinical, $N = 1,918$ across 5 international hospitals), preventing invalid data pooling.

• Leakage-Free Nested Pipelines: All imputation, feature engineering, and scaling are encapsulated exclusively within training partitions during cross-validation.

• Deep Tabular vs. Gradient Boosting Benchmark: Rigorous 1,000-iteration paired bootstrap hypothesis tests comparing tree-based algorithms with deep tabular neural baselines.

• Leave-One-Source-Out Generalization Audits: Quantitative stress-testing across hospital jurisdictions to measure transportability decay and covariate shift.

• Clinical Decision Curve Analysis: Evaluation of operational net clinical benefit across diagnostic thresholds $p_t \in [0.10, 0.90]$.

II. Related Work

Classical cardiovascular risk estimation began with the landmark Framingham Heart Study [2], establishing multivariable Cox proportional hazards models based on age, systolic blood pressure, smoking status, and cholesterol fractions. While interpretable, these linear risk scores assume constant hazard ratios across all demographic strata.

The advent of non-linear ensemble models, notably Random Forests [5] and Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (XGBoost) [4], substantially enhanced risk discrimination. Recent empirical studies by Shwartz-Ziv and Armon [11] and Grinsztajn et al. [12] demonstrated that decision tree ensembles consistently outperform deep neural networks on tabular datasets, owing to their inductive bias toward unrotated, axis-aligned hyperplanes characteristic of physiological cutoffs.

In clinical utility evaluation, Vickers and Elkin [6] established Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) to bridge the gap between statistical discrimination (ROC-AUC) and operational medical decisions. DCA explicitly integrates the clinical harm of false positives (unwarranted invasive angiograms) against false negatives (missed myocardial infarctions) [7].

III. Cohorts and Methodological Integrity

A. Cardio70k Primary-Care Screening Cohort

The Cardio70k cohort consists of $N = 68,581$ clean patient records derived from primary-care screening examinations. The dataset exhibits a balanced target distribution with 34,652 negative cases (50.53%) and 33,929 positive cases (49.47%). Demographically, the cohort includes 44,665 females (65.1%) and 23,916 males (34.9%), spanning 12 physiological predictors: age, biological sex, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pulse pressure, blood pressure classification category, total cholesterol level, glucose level, smoking status, alcohol consumption, and physical activity index.

B. Unified Clinical Multi-Center Cohort

The Unified Clinical cohort comprises $N = 1,918$ high-acuity diagnostic patients collected across five hospital centers in four countries:

1) Mendeley Data India: $N = 1,000$ South Asian patients (420 negative, 580 positive).

2) UCI Cleveland Clinic Foundation (USA): $N = 303$ patients (164 negative, 139 positive) [15].

3) UCI Hungarian Institute of Cardiology (Hungary): $N = 293$ patients (187 negative, 106 positive) [15].

4) UCI Long Beach Veterans Administration Medical Center (USA): $N = 199$ patients (51 negative, 148 positive) [15].

5) UCI University Hospital of Zurich (Switzerland): $N = 123$ patients (8 negative, 115 positive) [15].

Clinical predictors include resting blood pressure, serum cholesterol, fasting blood sugar, resting electrocardiography, maximum exercise heart rate, exercise-induced ST depression (oldpeak), and exercise angina.

C. Multimodal Asset Auditing and Exclusion Protocol

In preliminary data exploration, two supplementary archives were systematically audited: a 4,998-record ECG signal repository (`archive (3).zip`) and a 30,352-slice synthetic cardiac CT/MRI imaging archive (`archive (4).zip`). Data provenance verification revealed that both archives lacked universal, anonymized patient identification keys linking signals or images to the validated tabular clinical outcomes. Attempting synthetic cross-modal matching would introduce severe data fabrication and catastrophic target leakage. Consequently, in strict compliance with TRIPOD standards [13], both external repositories were excluded from supervised model training.

IV. System Architecture and Pipeline

To prevent information contamination, all preprocessing transformations were encapsulated within strict scikit-learn cross-validation pipelines:

1) Missingness Handling: Training-fold median imputation was applied for continuous biomarkers, paired with binary missingness indicators to capture potential informative missingness (e.g., Zurich cholesterol missingness at 68.3%).

2) Standard Scaling: Robust $z$-score normalization was computed exclusively on training partitions: $$z = \frac{x - \mu_{\mathrm{train}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{train}}}$$

3) Benchmarked Model Architectures: • $\ell_2$-Regularized Logistic Regression: $$P(Y=1|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b)}}$$ • Random Forest: 300 bagged trees with balanced class weighting [5]. • Histogram Gradient Boosting: Fast binned decision trees with early stopping. • XGBoost: Gradient boosted trees optimized with maximum tree depth 4, learning rate $\eta = 0.05$, and subsample ratio $0.80$ [4]. • Deep Tabular MLP: A regularized feedforward neural network comprising two hidden layers ($128 \to 64$ units) with ReLU activations, dropout ($p = 0.20$), and Adam optimization.

XGBoost attained superior discriminative performance across all evaluation metrics, achieving a mean ROC-AUC of $0.8019 \pm 0.0027$, PR-AUC of $0.7828$, and lowest calibration Brier score of $0.1802$.

Fig. 1. Discrimination curves on Cardio70k ($N=68,581$). Left: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves across all benchmarked models; Right: Precision-Recall (PR) curves confirming XGBoost champion separation.

B. Paired Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing

To rigorously determine whether XGBoost's empirical lead over the deep tabular neural network was statistically significant, we executed a 1,000-iteration paired bootstrap hypothesis test on held-out predictions: $$\Delta\mathrm{ROC\text{-}AUC} = \mathrm{ROC\text{-}AUC}_{\mathrm{XGBoost}} - \mathrm{ROC\text{-}AUC}_{\mathrm{MLP}}$$

The test confirmed a statistically significant performance advantage for XGBoost: $\Delta\text{ROC-AUC} = +0.0027$ with an empirical 95% bootstrap confidence interval of $[0.0020, 0.0036]$ and paired two-tailed $p < 0.001$. This empirically corroborates findings by Grinsztajn et al. [12] that decision tree inductive biases remain superior to feedforward neural architectures on tabular biomedical registries.

C. Probability Calibration

Reliable clinical risk communication requires well-calibrated probabilities. Brier score decomposition [8] and 10-bin Expected Calibration Error (ECE) were evaluated on out-of-fold predictions.

Fig. 2. Reliability calibration curves and predicted probability histograms. XGBoost closely aligns with the ideal diagonal (slope 1.0019, ECE 0.0024) on Cardio70k.

On Cardio70k, XGBoost demonstrated near-perfect calibration, exhibiting an empirical calibration slope of $1.0019$, an intercept of $+0.0002$, and an ECE of $0.0024$.

D. Leave-One-Source-Out Generalization Audits

To simulate real-world cross-hospital deployment, models were trained on four centers and tested on the fifth unseen center using the Unified Clinical cohort ($N = 1,918$). Results are detailed in Table II.

Fig. 3. Multi-center generalization degradation across held-out clinical sources. While European cohorts achieve ROC-AUC > 0.83, discrimination collapses to 0.4937 on the South Asian cohort.

The LOSO evaluation uncovers profound cross-site generalization decay. While models transferred effectively across Western cohorts (ROC-AUC $0.8370$ in Hungary and $0.8358$ in Cleveland), discrimination collapsed to near-random ($0.4937$ ROC-AUC) on the Indian cohort. This demonstrates that models trained on Western hospital schemas experience severe clinical covariate shift when applied to South Asian epidemiological distributions.

VI. Interpretability, Clinical Utility, and Equity

A. Clinical Decision Curve Analysis

Following the Vickers framework [6], [7], Net Clinical Benefit was computed across operational threshold probabilities $p_t \in [0.10, 0.90]$: $$\mathrm{Net\ Benefit} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{N} - \frac{\mathrm{FP}}{N}\left(\frac{p_t}{1 - p_t}\right)$$

Fig. 4. Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) on held-out Cardio70k validation data. The champion XGBoost model (solid blue curve) demonstrates superior Net Clinical Benefit across operational screening thresholds ($p_t \in [0.10, 0.90]$) compared to default "Treat All" (dashed gray) and "Treat None" (horizontal black line) strategies.

At a primary-care triage threshold of $p_t = 0.30$, XGBoost delivered a Net Benefit of $+0.3246$ compared to $+0.2782$ for "Treat All" and $0.000$ for "Treat None". At $p_t = 0.50$, universal intervention becomes clinically harmful ($\mathrm{NB} = -0.0105$), whereas XGBoost preserves a strong positive benefit of $+0.2305$, demonstrating concrete clinical utility.

B. Model-Agnostic Feature Reliance

Permutation feature importance was evaluated across 5 stratified folds on Cardio70k by computing the degradation in ROC-AUC ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC}$) after randomly shuffling each feature vector.

Fig. 5. Permutation feature importance on Cardio70k. Systolic blood pressure ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC} = -0.1473$), age ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC} = -0.0371$), and cholesterol level ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC} = -0.0298$) are primary physiological drivers.

Systolic blood pressure emerged as the preeminent physiological predictor ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC} = -0.1473 \pm 0.0026$), followed by patient age ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC} = -0.0371 \pm 0.0009$) and total cholesterol level ($\Delta\mathrm{AUC} = -0.0298 \pm 0.0011$).

C. Algorithmic Equity and Subgroup Slicing

To verify demographic equity and check for algorithmic bias, out-of-fold predictions were stratified across sex and age groups. Table III details performance metrics with exact 95% Clopper-Pearson binomial confidence intervals [14].

*Note: 95% Confidence Intervals computed using exact Clopper-Pearson binomial fiducial limits. Performance remains highly balanced across biological sexes.

Discrimination remains remarkably consistent across biological sexes: females achieved $0.8036$ ROC-AUC while males achieved $0.7985$ ROC-AUC. Across age strata, higher disease prevalence in elderly patients ($\ge 60$) shifted sensitivity higher ($0.8709$) at the expense of specificity ($0.3683$), illustrating that age-adjusted decision thresholds are required in geriatric clinical practice.

VII. Discussion

Our empirical findings provide three vital conclusions for translational medical AI:

1) Tree Models Outperform Neural Networks on Clinical Tables: In concordance with Grinsztajn et al. [12], gradient boosted trees possess an optimal inductive bias for axis-aligned clinical thresholds (e.g., hypertension cutoffs at 140 mmHg systolic BP), outperforming tabular neural networks ($p < 0.001$).

2) The Danger of Naive Cohort Pooling: Concatenating multi-center registries creates an illusion of massive sample sizes while concealing critical cross-border distribution shifts.

3) Statistical Metric vs. Clinical Utility: High ROC-AUC alone is insufficient for clinical adoption; Decision Curve Analysis objectively identifies the operational threshold boundaries where automated ML triaging delivers positive net utility over standard care.

VIII. Limitations and Future Work

A. Limitations of Current Work

1) Retrospective and Prevalent Label Design: Both Cardio70k ($N = 68,581$) and Unified Clinical ($N = 1,918$) datasets are retrospective cross-sectional registries capturing clinical parameters at a single diagnostic or screening visit. Consequently, the models predict contemporaneous disease presence (prevalent disease classification) rather than true 5-year or 10-year prospective incident cardiovascular risk, which would require longitudinal follow-up cohorts such as the Framingham [2] or UK Biobank registries.

2) Informative Missingness and Indication Bias: In real-world clinical practice, diagnostic biomarkers are not omitted at random (MCAR); rather, missingness is driven by clinical indication (MNAR). In the University Hospital of Zurich cohort, severe missingness on serum cholesterol (68.3%) and fluoroscopy (61.8%) reflected institutional referral triage where invasive tests were prioritized only for high-acuity patients. While our training-fold median imputation with missingness indicators preserved predictive signal, it does not explicitly capture the subjective clinical decision-to-test rationale.

3) Absence of Verified Universal Patient Linkages for Multimodal Fusion: As demonstrated in our data audits, external 12-lead ECG time-series archives and synthetic CT/MRI imaging repositories lacked secure, anonymized universal patient identification numbers. Attempting synthetic or unverified cross-modal pairing would introduce catastrophic data leakage and fabricated correlations. Consequently, our study was deliberately constrained to tabular physiological and hemodynamic predictors.

4) Architectural Scope of Tabular Deep Learning: Our neural baseline was restricted to a regularized two-hidden-layer feedforward Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). While representative of standard tabular neural baselines, newer self-attention tabular architectures (e.g., FT-Transformer, TabNet, SAINT) were not benchmarked in this cycle due to high hyperparameter instability and severe computational overhead on smaller multi-center cohorts.

5) Cross-System Generalization Gap in South Asian Populations: Although the Unified Clinical cohort incorporates the Mendeley Data India cohort ($N = 1,000$), our Leave-One-Source-Out evaluation revealed that models trained on Western UCI centers collapsed to near-random discrimination on Indian patients (ROC-AUC $0.4937$). This underscores that models trained on Western clinical guidelines cannot be deployed in South Asian healthcare environments without localized fine-tuning and recalibration.

B. Future Research Directions

1) Prospective EHR Integration via HL7 FHIR Microservices: We plan to containerize the champion XGBoost model into an interoperable microservice compliant with the Health Level Seven Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (HL7 FHIR) standard. Deploying this pipeline in pilot hospital primary-care workflows will enable prospective assessment of clinician alert acceptance, diagnostic turnaround acceleration, and reduction in unwarranted downstream stress testing.

2) Benchmarking Specialized Tabular Transformers: We will extend our tabular deep learning track to systematically evaluate column-wise self-attention networks, specifically FT-Transformer and TabNet, utilizing masked feature reconstruction pre-training on large unlabeled health insurance registries before fine-tuning on clinical endpoints.

3) Federated Multi-Hospital Learning: To reconcile cross-border cohorts without violating patient privacy regulations (HIPAA, GDPR), future iterations will implement federated learning ($\mathrm{FedAvg}$) equipped with differential privacy ($\varepsilon, \delta$). This will allow multi-center collaborative training across Swiss, American, and Indian hospital networks without transmitting raw protected health information.

4) Dynamic Calibration and Human-in-the-Loop Deferral: We aim to couple conformal prediction intervals with uncertainty estimation to deploy a reject-option triage system. Patients falling within intermediate predicted probability bands ($\hat{p} \in [0.42, 0.58]$) will be automatically routed for secondary physician review and definitive non-invasive imaging.

5) Localized Clinical Adaptation for South Asian Populations: Given the acute generalization drop on the Mendeley Data India cohort, we will collaborate with regional Indian cardiology institutes to assemble a multi-center South Asian CVD registry, allowing fine-tuning of risk models on indigenous epidemiological distributions.

IX. Conclusion

This paper establishes a rigorous, leakage-safe, and explainable cardiovascular disease prediction framework. By enforcing strict cohort segregation, Leave-One-Source-Out multi-center testing, and Decision Curve Analysis, we demonstrate that gradient boosted decision trees achieve champion discrimination ($0.8019 \pm 0.0027$ ROC-AUC), statistically outperforming deep neural networks ($p < 0.001$), while delivering positive Net Clinical Benefit across primary-care screening cutoffs. Our findings demonstrate that methodological rigor, transparent calibration, and clinical utility must supersede architectural complexity in translational medical AI.
